title: The Factors That Matter: A Formula for Understanding China’s Use of Force Calculus Over Taiwan
gist: The paper builds an eight-variable formula for Beijing's Taiwan use-of-force calculus — PLA readiness, domestic stability and Xi's legacy internally; Taiwan's separation trajectory, external events, US intervention odds, allied willingness and Taiwanese deterrent capability externally — and argues no single trigger drives invasion, only the convergence of several. Its most actionable conclusions: PLA readiness is the key enabling variable but Xi's purges have thinned the bench of combat-experienced commanders, Taiwan remains the world's most important semiconductor chokepoint with a war potentially shrinking global GDP by nearly 10%, and China becomes most dangerous not at peak confidence but when it believes a favorable window is closing.

insights.claim: A Chinese decision to invade Taiwan would not be driven by a single trigger but by the interaction of eight variables — internally PLA readiness, domestic stability and Xi Jinping's leadership legacy; externally Taiwan's perceived permanent separation, external events, likelihood of US military intervention, allied willingness to respond, and Taiwan's own deterrent capabilities.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Gives an eight-input dashboard for pricing Taiwan risk instead of relying on single headlines like the 2027 date — each variable is separately monitorable.
insights.locator: III. A Formula for China's Calculus for Taiwan Invasion

insights.claim: The variables in the framework are dynamic, interconnected and based on Chinese leadership perceptions rather than objective reality, so accurate Western assessments of the military balance matter less than what Beijing believes about it.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Signalling and perception management become the operative levers of deterrence — which means rhetoric and posture changes are tradeable events, not noise.
insights.locator: Thus, the framework emphasizes that these variables are dynamic

insights.claim: PLA readiness is the most important enabling variable because it determines whether Chinese leaders believe military action is operationally feasible, but it is not sufficient on its own — a highly capable PLA only makes the military option more credible and available.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Do not treat PLA capability milestones as invasion forecasts; capability is a necessary but not sufficient condition, which argues against binary 2027 positioning.
insights.locator: First, PLA readiness is arguably the most important enabling variable

insights.claim: The most dangerous configuration is convergence: high PLA readiness, Chinese perceptions that Taiwan is moving irreversibly away from unification, declining expectations of US intervention, limited anticipated allied participation, and weak confidence in Taiwan's ability to hold out until help arrives.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: A five-condition checklist for escalating from background risk to acute risk — hedge costs should scale with how many boxes are ticked simultaneously.
insights.locator: Third, the most dangerous scenario is the convergence

insights.claim: Domestic stability functions as a threshold condition that cuts both ways: stability lets Beijing absorb sanctions and market disruption, while severe instability could either constrain Beijing or push leaders toward greater risk if nationalist mobilization looks like it would reinforce regime legitimacy.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Chinese economic deterioration is not unambiguously good news for Taiwan risk — the diversionary-war channel means weak growth can raise conflict odds.
insights.locator: Second, several variables function as prerequisites

insights.claim: Two competing academic theories about domestic conditions apply: one holds that domestic strength is a component of comprehensive national power that enables risk-taking, and the other — diversionary war theory — holds that vulnerable leaders launch wars of choice to distract from domestic problems.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Because both high and low stability can motivate force, Chinese macro data alone cannot be used as a directional Taiwan-risk signal.
insights.locator: Domestic Stability in the PRC (DS)

insights.claim: Taiwan remains the world's most important semiconductor chokepoint despite years of US and allied diversification efforts, because even with new fabs under construction in Arizona, Japan and Europe the most advanced manufacturing capacity and much of the associated packaging and supplier ecosystem remains concentrated on the island.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Fab diversification headlines have not reduced the concentration risk in leading-edge nodes and advanced packaging — the tail risk to global tech supply is intact.
insights.locator: Taiwan remains the world's most important semiconductor choke point

insights.claim: Some reports cited in the paper indicate a war over Taiwan involving the United States and China could cause the global economy to shrink by nearly 10 percent, and that a Taiwan crisis would cause far more global economic damage than a Strait of Hormuz disruption.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Anchors the magnitude: a Taiwan conflict is a ~10% global GDP event, an order of magnitude above the energy-chokepoint shocks markets have recently priced.
insights.locator: Endnotes / Some reports indicate that a war over Taiwan

insights.claim: Kinetic and cyberattacks on terrestrial, maritime and space-based communications, transportation and energy infrastructure in a Taiwan war would have crippling economic effects, with collateral disruption to global trade, investment and finance dwarfing the 1970s oil shocks, the 2008 financial crisis and the 2020 pandemic.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Sets the correct comparison set for scenario modelling — this is a bigger shock than any of the last fifty years' benchmark crises, including for satellite and subsea infrastructure.
insights.locator: Additionally, kinetic and cyberattacks

insights.claim: In an intense, protracted US-China conflict military and civilian casualties would likely reach levels not seen since 1945, and the belligerents hold the second and third largest nuclear arsenals in the world, with China's far smaller than the US stockpile.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: The nuclear asymmetry in Washington's favour is one reason both sides retain strong incentives to avoid escalation — a stabilizing factor to weigh against alarmist scenarios.
insights.locator: I. The Stakes

themes.theme: PLA readiness, purges and amphibious hard limits

insights.claim: Recent purges within the PLA have depleted its bench of senior officers with operational experience, with research indicating fewer senior commanders and Central Military Commission members retain wartime experience such as service in the 1979 Sino-Vietnam War.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Human-capital degradation in the PLA officer corps is a concrete near-term dampener on invasion feasibility — a factor that argues against 2027 timelines.
insights.locator: One component of PLA readiness is the quality of personnel

insights.claim: Xi's new wave of purges is likely to slow some weapons modernization programs, disrupt command structures and decision-making, and weaken morale, all of which would degrade the PLA's ability to fight in the near to medium term.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Provides a mechanism-level reason to expect Chinese defence-program slippage — relevant to timing assumptions for regional defence procurement cycles.
insights.locator: Finally, a long-term factor in Chinese domestic politics

insights.claim: The purges create a two-sided risk: they may force Beijing to exercise greater caution before an amphibious assault, or Xi may become impatient with readiness concerns and launch an invasion as a 'test' of PLA capabilities.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Weak PLA readiness is not automatically reassuring; the paper explicitly flags an impatience scenario that most consensus analysis omits.
insights.locator: In the years ahead, the purges raise fundamental questions

insights.claim: Beijing has rarely waited for favorable conditions before ordering the PLA into battle — intervening in Korea in 1950 after civil-war devastation, attacking India in 1962 just after purging its most senior officer, and sending an ill-prepared force into Vietnam in 1979 — so Chinese leaders may pursue war even with unfavourable domestic conditions and an unready military.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: The strongest contrarian point in the paper: readiness-based reassurance has a poor historical track record for China, so readiness gaps should not be treated as a hard constraint.
insights.quote: Now, as then, Chinese leaders may pursue war even if the domestic economic and political conditions appear unfavorable—and even if the PLA is not ready to fight.
insights.locator: Nevertheless, Beijing has rarely waited for the right conditions

insights.claim: Xi's 2027 PLA milestone — ensuring the force is fully capable of meeting the demands of modern warfare at the PLA's 100th anniversary — has been linked to a possible Taiwan invasion, but a US intelligence report cited in the paper says China is not committed to a 2027 Taiwan invasion.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Directly undercuts the 2027 invasion consensus; the milestone is a modernization benchmark, not an operational deadline.
insights.locator: PLA Readiness (PLA)

insights.claim: An amphibious invasion of Taiwan faces three hard obstacles: choreographing thousands of ships, aircraft and personnel fast enough to neutralize Taiwanese forces before US intervention; a mountainous coastline with limited viable landing beaches, rivers and dense urban areas; and a PLA largely untested in large-scale combat operations.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: The physical constraints mean any invasion attempt would be visible in advance through shipping and logistics mobilization — a monitorable early-warning channel.
insights.locator: However, the PLA faces major obstacles

insights.claim: PLA readiness is a composite of interdependent capabilities — integrating army, navy, air, rocket, logistics, cyber and information support forces with unity of command, platform interoperability, delegation and robust command-and-control — which was the main reason Xi launched unprecedented organizational reforms in 2015.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Joint-operations integration, not platform counts, is the metric that matters when assessing PLA progress; ship and missile tallies overstate capability.
insights.locator: In addition to having experienced commanders

themes.theme: Taiwan's separation trajectory and economic decoupling

insights.claim: Cross-Strait trade and investment flows have shrunk dramatically over the past five years as Taiwan pursued its own derisking policy toward mainland China, moving in the opposite direction from Beijing's strategy of using economic ties to bolster cross-Strait integration.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Economic interdependence — the traditional restraint on conflict — is eroding by Taiwanese design, which mechanically raises Beijing's perceived cost of inaction.
insights.locator: On the economic front, since former President Tsai became president in 2016

insights.claim: Beijing has shut down virtually all mechanisms of communication with President Lai Ching-te and the DPP because Lai has not affirmed the One China Principle or repeated the 1992 Consensus, removing the crisis-management channels that would matter most in an incident.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Absent communication channels convert small incidents into escalation risk — the single most underpriced structural feature of the current cross-Strait setup.
insights.locator: The ties between the CCP and the Democratic Progressive Party

insights.claim: Lai Ching-te has stated more unequivocally than previous Taiwanese presidents that Taiwan is 'of course' a country, labelled the mainland a 'foreign hostile force', instituted 17 national security measures against PRC espionage, reinstated military tribunals, restricted cross-Strait exchanges and expelled mainland spouses advocating reunification by force.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence Taipei is hardening its stance; to some observers in China this has already crossed Beijing's red lines, raising the baseline probability of coercive responses.
insights.locator: From China's perspective, Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te

insights.claim: A growing proportion of Taiwan's population identifies primarily as Taiwanese rather than Chinese, a trend Beijing scholars view as one of the most consequential long-term challenges to peaceful unification because it suggests the societal foundations for unification are eroding and the window is narrowing.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Identity trend data is a slow-moving but directional input into Beijing's urgency calculation — it only pushes one way, toward a closing window.
insights.locator: Within this factor, a key issue is the emergence

insights.claim: Recent polling trends show most Taiwanese do not support reunification, with the vast majority preferring to maintain the status quo indefinitely, maintain it and decide later, or maintain it while moving toward independence.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: No domestic Taiwanese constituency exists for a negotiated unification, which removes the peaceful path Beijing claims to prefer.
insights.locator: Equally significant is Taiwanese public opinion

insights.claim: If Xi concludes that all prospects for peaceful reunification are narrowing or have closed, he may turn to military force — and China's 2005 anti-secession law contains a clause permitting force 'if all avenues of peaceful reunification have been exhausted' that Chinese academics are increasingly citing to justify non-peaceful means.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: The legal predicate for force already exists; watch Chinese academic and official invocations of the exhaustion clause as a leading escalation indicator.
insights.locator: Thus, these variables collectively serve as crucial enabling factors

insights.claim: Xi has elevated resolution of the Taiwan question above previous PRC leaders by declaring that long-standing political differences over Taiwan should not be passed down from one generation to the next, indicating his patience is finite and legacy-driven.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Legacy motivation ties conflict risk to Xi's personal political timeline rather than to objective conditions — a reason risk does not simply decay with time.
insights.quote: The long-standing political differences (over Taiwan) should not be allowed to be passed down from one generation to the next.
insights.locator: Leadership Legacy (LL)

insights.claim: No Chinese leader including Xi has ever renounced the use of force to achieve reunification, and at the 20th Party Congress Xi said China would never promise to renounce force while reserving the option of taking all measures necessary.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: The credible military threat is permanent policy, not a phase — any analysis assuming Beijing will foreswear force is mispricing the structural baseline.
insights.locator: Neither he nor any of his predecessors have ever renounced the use of force

themes.theme: US resolve, strategic ambiguity and Trump risk

insights.claim: Biden broke with strategic ambiguity by stating explicitly on two occasions that the US military would intervene to defend Taiwan, while Trump has largely maintained ambiguity, saying he would not comment in order to preserve negotiating leverage.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Presidential rhetoric on Taiwan is a directly observable deterrence variable; the reversion from Biden's clarity to Trump's ambiguity is itself a risk-increasing change.
insights.locator: Role of U.S. Military Intervention on Taiwan's behalf

insights.claim: If Trump publicly signalled that Taiwan could be a bargaining chip — as some assessed he did during his May 2026 meeting with Xi Jinping — Xi might conclude Washington would not come to Taiwan's aid, for example via remarks alluding to Taiwan being part of China's territory or comparing Xi's designs on Taiwan to Putin's on Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: An offhand Trump remark at a summit is a genuine, low-probability-high-impact escalation trigger — summit transcripts are worth reading as risk events.
insights.locator: But if Trump were to publicly signal that Taiwan could be a bargaining chip

insights.claim: The PLA closely watches US Pacific Command posture, and a major change such as pulling back troops, reducing regional presence or de-emphasizing commitments to allies could give Xi and the PLA sufficient justification to conclude Washington would not credibly intervene over Taiwan.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: US force-posture announcements in the Indo-Pacific are direct inputs to Chinese risk assessment — treat any drawdown as a deterrence-degrading event.
insights.locator: Second, the PLA is particularly attuned to public statements

insights.claim: The United States is arguably the only power with both the military capability and intent to prevent a successful Chinese invasion of Taiwan, a reality Xi Jinping is likely well aware of.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Deterrence is effectively single-sourced to Washington, so US political commitment — not allied capability — is the variable that matters most.
insights.locator: In short, public statements by U.S. presidents

insights.claim: The 1979 Taiwan Relations Act requires the United States to maintain the military capacity to resist any resort to force or coercion jeopardizing the security or the social or economic system of the people on Taiwan, and presidents since have directed INDOPACOM to plan accordingly.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: A statutory floor under US involvement exists regardless of presidential rhetoric — relevant to assessing how much a single administration can actually walk away.
insights.quote: resist any resort to force or other forms of coercion that would jeopardize the security, or the social or economic system, of the people on Taiwan
insights.locator: The U.S. military posture is informed by the 1979 Taiwan Relations Act

insights.claim: The two external events most likely to prompt Chinese military action are a formal Taiwanese declaration of independence via referendum or presidential statement, and a fundamental change in US One China policy such as formal recognition, a Trump visit to Taiwan, a Lai visit to the US, formal US troop deployments, or new security guarantees.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: A concrete tripwire list; any of these headlines should be treated as a step-change in Taiwan risk rather than incremental news.
insights.locator: On the second point, the two external events most likely

insights.claim: Beijing studies the Ukraine war through the lens of US hegemony and is focused on battlefield developments in speed, autonomous systems and non-kinetic warfare, with recent conflicts in Iran and Venezuela providing additional data points on warfare and international responses.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Chinese doctrine is being updated in real time from Ukraine, Iran and Venezuela — each Western intervention outcome feeds directly into Beijing's Taiwan planning.
insights.locator: External Events (EE)

insights.claim: Japan is the most forward-leaning US ally on Taiwan, with Abe's formulation that a Taiwan emergency is a Japanese emergency and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi telling the Diet that a Chinese naval blockade of Taiwan would constitute a survival-threatening situation triggering Japan's right of collective self-defense.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: A named Japanese threshold — naval blockade — is now on the record, so a blockade scenario carries automatic Japanese escalation risk beyond a purely US-China clash.
insights.quote: a Taiwan emergency is a Japanese emergency
insights.locator: Willingness of U.S. Allies and Partners to Intervene

insights.claim: Japan has not issued a formal pledge to fight over Taiwan and its likely role is understood as enabling US operations through basing, logistics and rear-area support rather than guaranteeing direct combat participation.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Distinguishes rhetoric from commitment: Japanese bases matter operationally, but Japanese combat participation should not be assumed in scenario modelling.
insights.locator: However, Japan has not issued a formal pledge to fight

insights.claim: Australia's senior officials stress that Canberra would consult with Washington under the alliance framework rather than automatically commit forces, and Anthony Albanese has refused to answer hypothetical questions about Australia's role in a Taiwan conflict, though scholars continue exploring how AUKUS could enable Australian support.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Even America's closest allies retain conditionality, which is precisely the ambiguity Beijing may read as coalition weakness.
insights.locator: Australia has also signaled increasing alignment

insights.claim: The Philippines lies less than 170 kilometres from Taiwan and has a mutual defense treaty with Washington, so some scholars argue it would be dragged into a conflict by geographic proximity alone, while non-treaty partner Singapore could support US assets and evacuation operations.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Widens the geography of physical and economic disruption in a Taiwan war to Southeast Asian bases, shipping and financial hubs.
insights.locator: Finally, countries like the Philippines and Singapore

insights.claim: Despite hosting over 28,000 US troops and its proximity to Taiwan, the consensus among most scholars and policymakers is that South Korea is unlikely to play a meaningful role in a Taiwan contingency because of its focus on North Korea and the political capital involved.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Removes South Korea from the coalition-of-the-willing calculus, which narrows allied capability and weakens the deterrent picture Beijing sees.
insights.locator: While South Korea remains a key U.S. ally

insights.claim: Perceptions of US resolve condition allied behaviour: if Washington appears hesitant or divided, Beijing may infer that Japan, Australia, the Philippines and other partners would be even less likely to assume major risks.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: US credibility has a multiplier effect on the whole coalition — meaning a single US wobble degrades deterrence more than its direct capability implies.
insights.locator: Similarly, U.S. resolve shapes allied behavior

insights.claim: Taiwan's 2025 Quadrennial Defense Review prioritizes multi-domain denial and resilient defense — an asymmetric strategy geared toward protraction rather than offensive battlefield success, emphasizing dispersal, survivability, mobile anti-ship and air-defense systems, mines, unmanned platforms, hardened command-and-control and reserve mobilization.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Names the Taiwanese procurement categories that will absorb defence budget: mines, mobile launchers, drones and hardened C2, not large platforms.
insights.locator: Taiwanese Deterrent Capabilities (TDC)

insights.claim: How Taiwan spends on defense is more consequential than how much it spends, because capabilities that threaten PRC transport ships, ports and logistics impose disproportionate costs and prolong a conflict.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Reframes the headline Taiwanese defence-budget number as a poor metric; composition of procurement is the real deterrence variable to track.
insights.quote: In this sense, how Taiwan spends on defense is more consequential than how much it spends.
insights.locator: In this sense, how Taiwan spends on defense

insights.claim: The central question for Chinese planners is not whether the PLA can defeat Taiwan in aggregate but whether it can do so rapidly and decisively before Taiwanese resistance hardens or external intervention materializes, so improvements in Taiwan's defenses deter by raising the probability of a protracted war of attrition.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Deterrence works through denying speed, not denying victory — the correct lens for evaluating whether any given Taiwanese or US capability actually matters.
insights.locator: Here, the central question for Chinese planners

insights.claim: Taiwanese deterrent capabilities compound with US intervention expectations: a force that survives initial strikes gives Washington and partners more time and political space to intervene, whereas brittle Taiwanese defenses raise Beijing's perceived likelihood of a successful fait accompli.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Taiwanese resilience investment has a leveraged effect on deterrence because it changes two variables at once — the highest-return item in the whole framework.
insights.locator: These variables can also compound one another

insights.claim: China may become most dangerous not when it feels fully confident but when it believes a favorable opportunity is closing — if Beijing thinks it is approaching the peak of its relative advantage while Taiwanese identity hardens, US-Taiwan ties deepen and allied coordination improves.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Inverts the standard rising-power framing: peak-China arguments are escalation-bullish, not reassuring, which changes how to read Chinese economic and demographic deterioration.
insights.quote: China may become most dangerous not when it feels fully confident, but when it believes that a favorable opportunity is closing.
insights.locator: Finally, the variables may interact differently

insights.claim: Concrete signs that Xi and the PLA are losing patience would include removal of the word 'peaceful' from China's 'peaceful reunification' formula, a new white paper or policy document emphasizing a closing window for peaceful resolution, or more pronounced destabilizing military exercises near Taiwan.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Three specific, observable tripwires — rhetorical formula changes and white papers are cheap to monitor and would precede any operational move.
insights.locator: Conversely, Xi and the PLA may lose patience with Taiwan

insights.claim: If Beijing believes the balance of power continues to shift in its favour it may prefer patience, coercion and political warfare over military action, meaning gradual Chinese ascendancy is the lower-risk scenario for a Taiwan conflict.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Counterintuitive positioning implication: a confidently rising China is less likely to invade than a peaking one, so watch Chinese self-assessment rather than raw capability trends.
insights.locator: Finally, the variables may interact differently

insights.claim: Long-term scenarios that could reset the calculus include the United States reorienting its military posture away from the Indo-Pacific at some point in the coming decade, China suffering a serious economic downturn coupled with unfavorable demographics, and new military technologies such as AI fundamentally altering future leaders' calculations.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Names AI and demographics as regime-changing variables for the Taiwan risk model — a reason not to extrapolate current deterrence conditions past a few years.
insights.locator: V. Conclusion

insights.claim: If Taiwan were persuaded the United States was disengaging militarily from the Western Pacific it might become willing to compromise and begin substantive talks on the CCP's terms, or alternatively increase its own defensive capabilities and seek other security partners — though the paper judges Washington the indispensable nation here.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Signals a peaceful-accommodation path that would still be a strategic loss for the West and a major shift for semiconductor supply-chain governance.
insights.locator: Taiwan, if persuaded that the United States was disengaging

insights.claim: Beijing's Taiwan decision-making is a fluid cost-benefit calculation rather than a binary choice, so the likelihood of Chinese military action depends less on any single trigger than on Beijing's overall perception that the balance of urgency, capability and acceptable risk has shifted decisively toward force.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Argues against event-driven Taiwan trading; the signal to watch is the drift of the composite perception, not individual incidents.
insights.locator: Thus, the central analytical contribution of this framework
